title: The Samaritan Woman and the Official's Son
summary: Traveling through Samaria, Jesus rests at Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. Their conversation moves from well water to living water, from her marital history to the true worship of the Father in spirit and truth, and Jesus tells her plainly that he is the Messiah. She tells her town, many Samaritans believe, and they call him the Savior of the world. Back in Cana, Jesus heals a royal official's dying son at a distance, his second sign.
story: Jesus has been in Judea, where his disciples baptized more people than John, and now he returns to Galilee by way of Samaria. Chapter 3 showed a respected Jewish teacher who came at night and struggled to understand. Chapter 4 shows a Samaritan woman, an outsider in every way a Jewish teacher would notice, who meets Jesus at noon and becomes a witness to her whole town. The contrast is deliberate. The good news moves beyond Jerusalem's boundaries, anticipating the mission of Acts 1:8 to Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth. The chapter closes with a Gentile or Herodian official who believes Jesus' word without seeing, which completes the Cana-to-Cana section that began in chapter 2.
historical:
Samaria was the region between Judea and Galilee. After Assyria conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and its capital Samaria in 722 BC, it deported many Israelites and resettled the land with peoples from elsewhere (2 Kings 17). Jews later regarded the Samaritans as a mixed people with a corrupted religion; Samaritans regarded themselves as the true descendants of the northern tribes and faithful keepers of the Law of Moses. They built a temple on Mount Gerizim, which the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed in the late second century BC, deepening the hostility. Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture and looked for a coming figure, based on Deuteronomy 18:15-18, who would restore true worship. Many Galilean Jews traveled through Samaria to reach Jerusalem, since it was the direct route, though some avoided it.

Sychar was near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim. Genesis 33:19 records Jacob buying land at Shechem, and Joshua 24:32 says Joseph's bones were buried there. A deep well near the site has been identified as Jacob's well since at least the fourth century. The royal official was probably in the service of Herod Antipas, whom people popularly called king.
cultural:
Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans because they regarded Samaritans as ritually unclean, and a Jewish teacher did not normally speak alone with a woman in public, which is why the disciples are surprised. Jesus crosses both lines in asking her for a drink. Living water was an everyday phrase for flowing water from a spring or stream, as opposed to still water in a cistern. Jesus uses it for the gift of God, echoing Jeremiah 2:13, where the Lord calls himself the spring of living water.

Why the woman came at the sixth hour, about noon, is often discussed. Many preachers have said she came at midday to avoid other women because of her reputation, but the text does not say this; travelers commonly rested at midday, people drew water at various times, and noon also sets up a contrast with Nicodemus's night visit. The dispute over the right place of worship, Gerizim or Jerusalem, was the central religious disagreement between Samaritans and Jews. Harvest normally came about four months after sowing, and Jesus' saying about fields ripe for harvest may point to the Samaritans coming toward him across the fields as he speaks.
literary: The conversation with the woman is one of the longest dialogues in the Gospels, and it follows John's pattern of misunderstanding and revelation. She hears living water as flowing well water; Jesus means eternal life. She calls him a Jew, then Sir, then a prophet, and finally wonders whether he could be the Christ, while her townspeople confess him as the Savior of the world. His self-revelation, I who speak to you am He, is literally I am, the one speaking to you, the first of many I am sayings in John. A second misunderstanding follows with the disciples about food (verses 31 to 34), parallel to the first about water. The scene at the well also echoes Old Testament stories in which a man meets a woman at a well, as with Isaac's servant and Rebekah, Jacob and Rachel, and Moses and Zipporah, stories that led to marriage. Some readers see the bridegroom of 3:29 here, gathering a people to himself.

outline.t: Jesus travels through Samaria to Jacob's well
Worship in spirit and truth; I am He
The woman's witness; the fields ripe for harvest
The Samaritans believe: the Savior of the world
The official's son healed, the second sign

doctrines.note: Jesus teaches that the time is coming when true worship will not depend on a holy mountain or city but will be in spirit and truth. Worship is directed to the Father, enabled by the Spirit, and centered on the truth revealed in Jesus. The Father seeks such worshipers.

The chapter shows the gospel crossing ethnic, religious, and gender boundaries. A Samaritan woman becomes the first person in John's Gospel to bring a whole community to Jesus, and the Samaritans confess him as the Savior of the world.

Jesus reveals himself as the Messiah more directly to this Samaritan woman than to anyone else so far in John. He is the giver of living water, the one who knows people fully, and the Savior of the world, not only of Israel.

words.note: Proskuneō, to worship, originally to bow down or prostrate oneself before someone. It appears nine times in this chapter, more than anywhere else in the Gospels, because worship is the heart of the conversation. The question is no longer where to bow down, but how and to whom.

Alētheia, truth. In John truth is more than accurate information; it is the reality of God revealed in Jesus, who is full of grace and truth (1:14) and later says he is the truth (14:6). Worship in truth means worship that corresponds to who God really is as he has made himself known.

Pēgē, spring or fountain. It names Jacob's well in verse 6 (the well was spring-fed) and the fount of water springing up to eternal life in verse 14. Jesus contrasts water drawn with effort from a deep well with a spring that rises within, a picture John later connects with the Spirit (7:38-39).

Sōtēr, savior. The Samaritans call Jesus the Savior of the world. In the Roman world the title was used of gods and of emperors. The Samaritans give it to a Jewish teacher, a confession that his salvation reaches beyond Israel to all peoples.

christ: Jesus is shown here as fully human, tired and thirsty at a well at noon, and as the one who gives living water, eternal life, to all who ask. He knows the woman's life without being told, and she recognizes a prophet. He is the Messiah the Samaritans awaited, and he declares himself openly with words that echo God's own I am. He is also the one who, though salvation comes from the Jews, is the Savior of the whole world, and he shows it by breaking the barrier between Jew and Samaritan. His food is to do his Father's will and finish his work, a work he will complete on the cross, where he says, It is finished. In Cana, his word alone heals a dying boy far away, and the father believes before he sees.

hard.q: Was the Samaritan woman notoriously immoral, as she is often portrayed?
hard.a: Many sermons describe her as a woman of loose morals shunned by her town, but the text itself is more restrained, and interpreters read it in several ways. The traditional reading takes her five husbands and current partner as evidence of sexual sin, which Jesus gently exposes. Others point out that in her world only men could initiate divorce under Jewish law, and a woman might have been widowed several times or divorced by husbands for reasons that were not her fault, as in the Sadducees' story of the seven brothers (Luke 20:27-33). On this reading, the man she now has, who is not her husband, might be a relative who supports her, a levirate arrangement never formalized, or a partner she lives with out of necessity. A few interpreters take the five husbands symbolically, as the five peoples and their gods resettled in Samaria in 2 Kings 17, though most doubt this. Notice what the text does not say: Jesus does not call her a sinner or command her to repent, and she speaks with him as a serious theological conversation partner. Her townspeople listen to her testimony and come out to see him, which suggests she was not simply an outcast. Whatever her past, Jesus knows it fully and still offers her living water, and she becomes a witness.

questions: Jesus crossed barriers of ethnicity, religion, and gender to speak with this woman. What barriers would he ask you to cross?
The woman's message was simple: come and see a man who told me everything I ever did. What is the simplest honest thing you could say about what Jesus has done for you?
The official believed Jesus' word before he saw his son healed. Where do you need to take Jesus at his word?
